source.title: Building the System
source.summary: What an Islamic monetary system would look like, not at the bank level, but at the system level. Principles, obstacles, and the path forward.
source.author: Islamic Economics
source.body_text: Gold dinar revival proposals sound appealing but face practical limitations. This episode moves beyond nostalgia to ask what a modern Islamic monetary system would actually require: five design principles for an Islamic monetary authority, the question of OIC monetary cooperation, and why governance is the binding constraint, not monetary design. The principles exist, the capital exists, the technology exists, and the need is real. But building institutions requires the hardest thing of all: trust between governments that have rarely cooperated at this level.

linkedin.post: Beyond the Gold Dinar: What Islamic Monetary Cooperation Actually Requires Gold dinar revival proposals capture the imagination but miss the fundamental challenge. The latest Islamic Economics podcast episode cuts through the nostalgia to examine what a modern Islamic monetary system would actually require. The framework exists: five design principles for an Islamic monetary authority that could serve the Muslim world. The resources are available: sufficient capital pools across Islamic countries. The technology is proven: modern monetary systems work at scale. So what's missing? The episode identifies the binding constraint: governance and trust between governments that have rarely cooperated at the monetary level. Building institutions requires something harder than capital or technology—it requires sustained diplomatic coordination. The OIC monetary cooperation question isn't about returning to medieval trade systems. It's about whether Islamic countries can build the institutional trust necessary for monetary integration in the 21st century. Listen: https://islamiceconomics.github.io/podcast.html#ep-mm-6

The need is undeniable. But here's the constraint nobody talks about: trust between governments that have rarely cooperated at this level. The binding limitation isn't monetary design or returning to medieval trade systems. It's governance. It's building the institutional relationships necessary for true monetary cooperation. The question isn't whether Islamic countries should have their own monetary system. It's whether they can build the diplomatic trust required to make it work. short_video.hook: Everyone talks about the gold dinar, but they're missing the real constraint.
short_video.voiceover: Gold dinar proposals sound appealing because they feel principled and historical. But they miss the fundamental challenge. Five design principles exist for an Islamic monetary authority. The capital exists across Islamic countries. The technology works at scale. So what's the real constraint? Trust between governments that have rarely cooperated at this level. The binding limitation isn't monetary design or returning to medieval systems. It's governance. It's building the institutional relationships necessary for true cooperation. The hardest part isn't the economics. It's the politics.
